title: Sudoku Solver
description: Solve a 9×9 Sudoku by backtracking with row, column, and box constraint sets and minimum-candidate ordering.

data.text: Fill a partially completed 9×9 Sudoku grid so that every row, every column, and every 3×3 box contains the digits 1 through 9 exactly once. The puzzle is guaranteed to have a unique solution. Modify the board in place.
A board where row 0 is `["5","3",".",".","7",".",".",".","."]` and so on. The `.` characters mark empty cells to be filled.

For each empty cell in order, try every digit and check validity by scanning the whole row, column, and box — nine cells each. That is work repeated constantly, and it is the difference between a solver that finishes instantly and one that times out.

data.title: Backtracking with on-demand checks
data.content: Correct, but repeats the same scans at every level.

data.text: Track which digits are already used in each row, column, and box as bitmasks. Checking whether a digit is allowed becomes a single bitwise `AND`, and placing or removing a digit is a bitwise OR or XOR. The box index for cell `(r, c)` is `(r / 3) * 3 + c / 3`.

data.title: Bitmask solver — O(1) constraint checks
data.content: Three 9-element bitmask arrays make every validity check constant time.

data.title: Bitmasks turn three scans into one AND
data.text: `rows[row] | cols[col] | boxes[box]` is the set of digits already used in all three constraints. The test `(used & bit) != 0` is a single instruction instead of up to 27 comparisons.

data.title: Minimum remaining values dramatically prunes
data.text: Instead of filling the first empty cell, fill the empty cell with the **fewest legal candidates**. That is the classic MRV heuristic from constraint satisfaction. It can cut the search tree by orders of magnitude on hard puzzles at the cost of a scan per level — well worth it.

data.title: Backtracking must undo every mask, not just the cell
data.text: If you reset `board[row][col]` to `'.'` but forget to clear the three bitmasks, later digits will be rejected for reasons that no longer apply, and the solver will report a puzzle unsolvable when it is not.

data.caption: The solver fills one empty cell at a time; a dead end returns false and the caller restores the cell and its three masks.
data.definition:
graph TD
    A["find empty cell"] --> B["used = row | col | box"]
    B --> C["try each digit not in used"]
    C --> D["place, update masks, recurse"]
    D --> E["dead end? return false"]
    E --> F["restore cell and masks, try next digit"]
    F --> C
    C --> G["all digits fail -> return false"]
    D --> H["no empty cells -> solved"]
    style H fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32

cards.title: On-demand validity scans
cards.description: Check the row, column and box each time

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: Sudoku is the reference example of constraint-satisfaction backtracking, and the two upgrades here — cheap constraint representation and the minimum-remaining-values heuristic — are the two levers that make any CSP solver practical. The same shape solves graph colouring, timetable scheduling, and the N-Queens variant that places many queens.
